planting.note: Detach rooted basal offsets once they reach roughly a third the size of the parent rosette and pot into coarse, fast-draining bromeliad mix.

directions: A variegated selection of Neoregelia compacta, 'Bossa Nova' forms a broad, stoloniferous rosette of light green leaves crisply edged in cream-white, the whole center flushing brilliant red as the plant matures toward bloom. It spreads slowly by runners into a colony rather than a single clump, so give it room or plant it where offsets can be shared out. Bright filtered light keeps the margins crisp and the red blush strong; too much shade dulls the variegation to plain green while harsh midday sun can scorch the pale edges. Keep the central cup topped up with water and flush it periodically to prevent stagnation, and use an open, chunky bark-based mix that drains fast around the roots.

common_name: Del Mar Aechmea (Blue-Pink Landscape Urn Bromeliad)

planting.note: Separate basal pups once they have several leaves and some root development, then pot into coarse, free-draining bromeliad mix.

directions: A popular landscape and interior hybrid, Aechmea 'Del Mar' forms a broad rosette of light green, leathery, lightly spined leaves that set off its show-stopping inflorescence: a hot-pink flower spike rising well above the foliage, wrapped in brilliant cobalt-blue-purple floral bracts. It flowers reliably in warm, bright, filtered-light conditions and holds color for weeks, making it a favorite for tropical border plantings in frost-free climates as well as patio containers further north. Keep the central tank filled with fresh water and flush it regularly, and grow it in a chunky, well-drained bark or bromeliad mix that never stays soggy at the roots.

planting.note: Remove rooted offsets from the base of the spent rosette and mount or pot in an open, epiphyte-style bark mix.

directions: Raised by Mulford Foster in 1945 from Aechmea orlandiana crossed with Aechmea fosteriana and named for his son, 'Bert' forms an open, upright vase of matte green leaves marked with irregular purplish-brown crossbands and fine marginal spines. In bloom it sends up an arching inflorescence carrying a dense panicle of red bracts and small yellow petals, a striking contrast against the banded foliage. As an epiphytic hybrid it does best mounted on bark or grown in a very open, fast-draining bromeliad mix under bright filtered light, which intensifies the crossbanding. Keep the central cup filled with fresh water and let the roots dry between waterings if potted.

planting.note: Divide rooted offsets from the base of the rosette in spring and let cuts callus a day before potting into very gritty, fast-draining soil.

directions: Unusual among Dyckia hybrids for its unarmed leaf margins, 'Naked Lady' forms a recurving rosette of smooth-edged, light green to yellow-green leaves that still taper to a sharp, spine-tipped point. Unlike tank-forming bromeliads, Dyckia is a terrestrial genus that takes up water and nutrients through its roots rather than a central cup, so it wants gritty, mineral, cactus-style soil and full sun rather than shaded cup-watering culture. Established plants in strong light send up slender, wand-like flower stalks carrying small orange blooms in spring that draw hummingbirds. It works well in a rock garden, xeriscape bed, or shallow container where its smooth foliage and recurved form can be appreciated up close without the hazard of typical Dyckia spines.

planting.note: Detach rooted basal offsets once they reach a third to half the size of the parent and pot into a loose, bark-based bromeliad mix.

directions: Bred by Cornelius Bak from Vriesea splendens, 'Splenriet' keeps the flaming sword's dramatic strap-shaped, softly banded foliage while offering a more compact, floriferous habit. Its tall, sword-like flower spike opens in vivid color above the rosette and holds for weeks, making it one of the longer-blooming Vriesea hybrids in general cultivation. Grow it in mostly shade to bright, indirect light — direct sun quickly scorches the leaves — and keep the central cup filled with fresh water, flushing periodically to prevent stagnation. An airy, well-drained bark-based mix and steady warmth mimic the humid understory conditions this hybrid's parent species favors.

common_name: Domingos Martins Billbergia (White-Blotched Banded Tube Bromeliad)

planting.note: Separate large rooted offsets from the base of the tubular rosette and pot into an open, fast-draining bromeliad mix.

directions: Collected near Domingos Martins, Brazil and introduced to cultivation by Bob Whitman in the 1980s, this Billbergia vittata selection has become one of the most influential parent plants in modern Billbergia hybridizing. It forms an upright, tubular rosette of dark-spined, banded leaves that develop heavy white blotching as the plant matures, giving mature specimens a strikingly marbled look distinct from the plainer species form. Bright filtered light brings out the strongest banding and blotch contrast, while deep shade fades it toward plain green. As with other tank bromeliads, keep the central tube filled with fresh water and grow it in a coarse, well-drained bark mix that allows the roots to dry between waterings.

planting.note: Detach rooted basal offsets from the compact tubular rosette and pot into a loose, fast-draining bromeliad mix.

directions: Raised by Don Beadle from a cross of Billbergia 'Domingos Martins' and 'Ed McWilliams,' 'Hallelujah' is a compact tubular hybrid whose leaves blend red, pink, purple, and white in translucent patches that glow when backlit by the sun. Color saturates best in strong filtered light or a few hours of gentle direct sun, while its small, upright habit suits patio containers as readily as garden beds in frost-free climates. Short-lived but eye-catching red, white, and blue-toned flowers can appear at almost any time of year from the central tube. Keep the tank topped up with fresh water and grow in a coarse, well-drained bromeliad or bark-based mix.

common_name: Orange Star Guzmania (Long-Lasting Orange Bract Bromeliad)

planting.note: Remove rooted basal offsets after the parent rosette finishes blooming and pot into a light, fast-draining bromeliad mix.

directions: Bred by Deroose Nurseries from Guzmania lingulata, 'Orange Star' produces a compact rosette of glossy green leaves topped by a star-shaped arrangement of bright orange bracts surrounding small, inconspicuous true flowers. The bract display is exceptionally long-lasting, often holding color for several months, which has made it a mainstay of the interior-plantscaping trade as well as a shaded patio accent in frost-free climates. Grow it in bright, indirect light or dappled shade — direct sun bleaches the bracts and scorches the foliage — and keep the central cup filled with fresh, room-temperature water, flushing it occasionally. A light, well-aerated bromeliad or orchid-bark mix suits its modest root system.
